newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Islamic summit condemns Isreali settlement policy.
newsitem.headline: Islamic summit condemns Isreali settlement policy.

text.p: Islamic leaders condemned Israel's "expansionist" settlement policies on Sunday and asked Moslem states to review their ties with the Jewish state.

A one-day summit of the 54-member Organisation of Islamic Conference, called to mark Pakistan's 50 years of independence, urged the world to compel Israel to implement in full all its agreements in the Middle East peace process.

The OIC strongly condemned "Israel's persistence in its settlement expansionist policies in Al-Quds al-Sharif (Jerusalem) and the rest of the occupied Palestinian and Arab territories," said a declaration adopted at the end of the meeting.

It urged member states to "review relations with Israel and make them contingent on the progress achieved in the peace process, and on the extent to which Israel complies with U.N. resolutions and with agreements, commitments and obligations reached by the parties concerned".
The summit also adopted a general "Islamabad declaration" pledging to broaden and deepen co-operation among OIC states in "all affairs".
It said the member states agreed to "co-operate in all efforts to eradicate the phenomenon of terrorism" and strengthen economic and commercial cooperation.

The summit also declared support for a "just and peaceful solution" of Pakistan's dispute with India over the Himalayan region of Kashmir under U.N. resolutions which envision a plebiscite there, and called for an early political reconciliation in war-shattered Afghanistan.
The summit took place in a round convention centre built for the occasion by the government of ousted prime minister Benazir Bhutto, who not present at the among guests at the opening.
Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat used the opening session to attack what he called Israeli aggression.
Arafat said Israeli "obstinacy and intransigence" had frozen peace negotiations with Syria and Lebanon and was hindering those with the Palestinians.
"We were surprised by the Israeli decision to isolate and Judaise Jerusalem, constructing new settlements not only inside it but outside it," Arafat said.

Israeli-Palestinian tension has been high since right-wing Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Natanyahu sent bulldozers last Tuesday to a hill between Jerusalem and Bethlehem to begin a new Jewish settlement in territory occupied by Israel.
A suicide bombing, claimed by the radical Moslem Hamas group, killed three Israeli women in Tel Aviv on Friday.
Arafat accused Israel of delaying implementation of agreements with the Palestinians to "please right-wing Israeli religious parties which are hostile to the peace process".
Speaking for the Arab group at the OIC, Arafat criticised the United States for vetoing a U.N. Security Council resolution demanding that Israel halt the East Jerusalem settlement.
"Unfortunately the veto of the United States, twice, only helped encourage Israel to pursue its aggression and its challenge to international legitimacy," Arafat said.
Pakistani President Farooq Leghari, in his inaugural speech, said his country wanted good relations with its arch-rival India, but their dispute over Kashmir must be solved.
"A just solution of the Kashmir dispute, in accordance with U.N. resolutions, is essential to ease tensions which have afflicted relations between Indian and Pakistan," Leghari said.
Pakistan's Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif also spoke of the need for an "honourable settlement" of the Kashmir dispute.
"We have decided to resume bilateral talks with India in the hope that India would reciprocate this gesture," he said.
Top officials of the Indian and Pakistani foreign ministries are due to meet in New Delhi from March 28 to 31 to renew a dialogue that foundered over Kashmir in January 1994.
